interview_metadata.name: Janell Porterfield
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born in Norwich, New York, but I have lived in Sherburne basically my whole life. It is small enough that people know your car before they know your name, and if something is happening at school or at the fairgrounds everybody hears about it. My parents raised me to keep busy and follow through on what I said I would do, so I have always been the kid with a planner and color-coded folders. When I was little I was into animals first, like I would check out books about wolves and birds and make little fact pages. Then in elementary school I started piano, and later I got into soccer because a few girls from my class were playing and I wanted to be with them. Middle school is where things got more like my life now. I got serious about soccer, joined drama club, started doing student council, and learned Python from online tutorials and school projects. I like math and science a lot, but I also like performing and making videos, so I do not really fit into just one group. A big thing for me was becoming captain on the middle school soccer team, because I had to stop only worrying about how I played and start noticing if a younger player was nervous or if somebody was left out. Another big thing was doing The Crucible in school drama, because it made me realize I could be loud and expressive in front of people instead of just organized behind the scenes. My family is close. My mom and dad come to games and concerts when they can, and my younger brother is annoying but also funny. I have friends from soccer, drama, student council, and the animal shelter, and sometimes I feel like my whole life is moving between practices, homework, rehearsals, and whatever project I decided to make harder than it needed to be.

follow_ups.question: What is one ordinary childhood memory that feels very Sherburne to you?
follow_ups.response: Going to the county fair with my family and seeing people from school, church, soccer, and the farmers' market all in one place. I remember eating fries, taking pictures of the animals, and my mom stopping every five feet to talk to someone.

follow_ups.question: When did coding become part of your life?
follow_ups.response: Around sixth grade, when we did a little coding activity in school and I got hooked on making the computer actually do what I told it to do. I made a tiny Python quiz game first, then a homework tracker because I kept forgetting which assignment was for which class.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: For me it was probably deciding whether to stay with soccer when it started getting more serious. In sixth grade I was doing piano, drama, student council, and schoolwork, and soccer club practices with Adirondack United were making my weeks really packed. I remember one week I had a math test, rehearsal, a game, and a video project due, and I cried in the car because I thought I had to quit something. My dad said quitting was allowed, but I had to know if I was quitting because I did not love it or because I was disorganized. That bothered me, because I am the organized person. So I made this big schedule on Google Calendar, talked to my coach, and decided to keep soccer but be more honest about homework time. After that I became more disciplined. It also made me see that I like being part of teams, even when it is stressful.

follow_ups.question: Who helped you think through that choice the most?
follow_ups.response: My dad helped with the practical part, and my mom helped with the emotional part. My friend Avery from soccer also helped because she said she would miss me if I quit, and that made it feel real.

follow_ups.question: What changed after you chose to stay with soccer?
follow_ups.response: I started packing my soccer bag the night before, doing homework in study hall, and blocking Sunday afternoon for bigger assignments. I also stopped saying yes to every little extra thing unless I checked my week first.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was a conscious choice. I sat at the kitchen table with my planner and actually decided that soccer was worth making room for.

follow_ups.question: Did it feel like a grown-up decision?
follow_ups.response: A little, yes, because no one forced me either way. My parents made me own the decision.

follow_ups.question: Do you still use that same decision-making style?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I write things out. If I can see the week on paper, I usually calm down.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Maybe the school could make it easier for kids who do a lot of activities to know deadlines earlier. Mostly, though, having coaches and teachers who understand when weeks get packed helps.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would actually work?
follow_ups.response: A shared activity calendar would help, so drama, sports, and student council are not all scheduling big things on the same day.

follow_ups.question: Did any adult at school help?
follow_ups.response: My science teacher let me ask questions during lunch before a test, and that made the week less awful.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I definitely do not have a partner or children. I am thirteen, so my family is my parents, my brother, my grandparents, and a couple of cousins I see a lot. My mom, Karen, is the person I talk to when I am stressed or when something social happens at school and I need help figuring out if I am overthinking it. She also knows animals really well, so I probably get my veterinary and wildlife interests from her. My dad, Mike, is more practical and calm. He fixes things, drives me to soccer, and always asks what the actual problem is before I start spiraling. My younger brother Tyler is nine, and we fight over the TV and snacks, but I help him with homework and he comes to some of my games. My grandparents live close enough that we see them for Sunday dinners sometimes, and my grandma asks about every rehearsal like it is Broadway. Family is important to me because in a small town your family is also part of your schedule, your rides, your traditions, and who shows up when you need something.

follow_ups.question: What does a normal family evening look like at your house?
follow_ups.response: Usually dinner around 6:30 if practice does not mess it up, then homework at the kitchen table or in my room. My dad watches sports, Tyler plays games, and my mom is usually folding laundry or asking everyone what forms need signing.

follow_ups.question: Who in your family do you spend the most one-on-one time with?
follow_ups.response: Probably my mom on regular days, but my dad during soccer season because of all the driving. Some of our best talks happen in the car after practice.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: We also have our dog, Scout, who feels like immediate family even though he is not a person. My aunt Lisa and cousin Maddie are close too, and Maddie is almost like an older sister when she visits.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your cousin Maddie?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once or twice a month, more in summer. She helps me with makeup for performances because I am not very good at it.

follow_ups.question: What role does Scout have in the house?
follow_ups.response: He is basically the emotional support dog for everybody. He sits under the table when I do homework.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: My closest friends are Avery from soccer, Mia from drama, and Sophie from student council. Avery is competitive and funny, so she pushes me during practice. Mia is more dramatic in the best way and always has ideas for costumes or videos. Sophie is organized like me, so we can actually run a meeting without it becoming chaos. I also like the people at the animal shelter where I volunteer sometimes on Saturdays. There is one older volunteer, Mrs. Daniels, who lets me help refill water bowls and talks to me about what it is like to work with animals.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your friends outside school?
follow_ups.response: Avery I see at soccer two or three times a week in season. Mia and Sophie I mostly see at school, but we text and sometimes hang out after rehearsals or meetings.

follow_ups.question: Do you have a romantic partner?
follow_ups.response: No. People in eighth grade talk about dating, but I am not really doing that.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: We live in Sherburne, which is in Chenango County and feels very upstate New York. There are houses with yards, older buildings, fields not too far away, and a lot of people who have lived here forever. It is not like there is a mall or a huge movie theater nearby, so people do school events, sports, church dinners, farmers' markets, and county fair stuff. I like that I can recognize people at the grocery store, and my parents usually know whose parent is coaching what. It can feel quiet, but I like quiet when I am doing homework or editing videos. The best part is being close to trails and being able to take weekend trips toward the Adirondacks or Catskills.

follow_ups.question: Where do you spend time around town?
follow_ups.response: School is the main place, then the soccer field, the library sometimes, and the animal shelter. I also go to the farmers' market with my mom when it is running.

follow_ups.question: What does your street feel like?
follow_ups.response: Pretty calm. You hear lawn mowers, dogs, and trucks more than anything exciting.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel pretty safe. My parents still want to know where I am, but I do not feel scared walking with friends near school or being outside in our yard.

follow_ups.question: Are there places you avoid?
follow_ups.response: Not really, except I do not walk alone at night because my parents would not like that and I would feel weird anyway.

follow_ups.question: What makes it feel safe?
follow_ups.response: People know each other, and if something unusual happened, somebody would probably notice.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The good part is community and nature. The hard part is there are not endless things to do, and sometimes everyone knowing everyone means rumors move fast.

follow_ups.question: What do you wish Sherburne had more of?
follow_ups.response: More teen spaces, like a good cafe where you could do homework and not feel like you are in the way.

follow_ups.question: What would you miss if you moved?
follow_ups.response: The fields, my school people, and how easy it is to be involved in things.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Right now it is me, my mom Karen, my dad Mike, and my younger brother Tyler. My mom works during the week and keeps the family calendar together. My dad works full time too and does a lot of driving for my soccer and school stuff. Tyler is in elementary school, and he is into video games and drawing monsters. We also have Scout, our dog, but no extra people staying with us right now.

follow_ups.question: Who is usually home first after school or work?
follow_ups.response: I get home after school unless I have practice. My mom is usually home before my dad, but it depends on the day.

follow_ups.question: Where do you usually do homework at home?
follow_ups.response: At the kitchen table if I need help, or at my desk if I need quiet. My desk is neater than my locker.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone is permanent. No one is just staying temporarily.

follow_ups.question: Has anyone stayed temporarily before?
follow_ups.response: Only relatives visiting for a night or two, not really living with us.

follow_ups.question: Does your cousin ever stay over?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes Maddie sleeps over, but just for fun.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: My cousin Maddie might stay over on a weekend, and sometimes my grandma stays late after dinner, but no regular extra person.

follow_ups.question: How often are sleepovers?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once a month or less, usually during school breaks.

follow_ups.question: Do friends stay over too?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes Mia or Avery, but my parents like planning it ahead.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, everyone who usually lives here is here.

follow_ups.question: Any family members away at college?
follow_ups.response: Not in my household. Some older cousins are, though.

follow_ups.question: Anyone away for medical care?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: School days start around 6:30. I get ready, eat cereal or toast, and get to school around 7:45. During the day I have classes, lunch with friends, and usually try to finish some homework in study hall. After school depends on the season. In soccer season I have school practice or Adirondack United practice a few days a week, and in drama season I might have rehearsal until about 5:00 or 5:30. Student council is usually once a week, and piano practice is at home most evenings for 20 or 30 minutes. Saturdays might be a game, animal shelter volunteering, hiking with family, or editing a video. Sundays are homework, laundry, sometimes church with my family, and trying to reset my backpack.

follow_ups.question: What is your busiest day of the week?
follow_ups.response: Tuesday is usually the worst because I can have student council, soccer, and a bigger homework load.

follow_ups.question: What do you do right before bed?
follow_ups.response: I check my planner, put my Chromebook on the charger, and usually listen to Billie Eilish or read a mystery book for a little bit.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I do not have a paid job because I am thirteen. My job is basically school, activities, and helping at home. I do volunteer at the animal shelter sometimes on Saturdays, usually for a couple hours if my mom can drive me. I help with simple things like water bowls, folding towels, cleaning up, and sometimes socializing cats if they say it is okay. I also do student council work, like taking meeting notes or helping plan a food drive, but that is not paid. If I earn money, it is from chores or birthday money, not a regular job.

follow_ups.question: What chores do you do at home?
follow_ups.response: Dishes, feeding Scout, folding my laundry, and sometimes helping Tyler clean up if he is making everyone crazy.

follow_ups.question: Would you want a paid job later?
follow_ups.response: Yes, maybe at a vet clinic, farm stand, library, or something with animals when I am old enough.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I keep track of a lot of small responsibilities. I pack my soccer gear, charge my school laptop, keep student council minutes, and remind people in group projects what their part is. At home I feed Scout in the morning if my brother forgets, and I help make dinner sometimes, especially pizza or chicken teriyaki stir-fry. I also try to practice piano before I get too tired. My locker is the one place where my system fails, because I have been known to hide snack wrappers in there until it is disgusting.

follow_ups.question: What is your most regular responsibility?
follow_ups.response: Checking my planner every night. If I skip that, the next day is usually messier.

follow_ups.question: What dinner do you actually like making?
follow_ups.response: Homemade pepperoni pizza. I like putting basil on it if we have fresh basil from the school garden.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The biggest change is when the season changes. When soccer is active, my afternoons are practice and games, and I am more tired at night. During drama season, rehearsals take over and I have to memorize lines instead of running drills. Recently I have also been trying to code more consistently, even if it is just 20 minutes, because I want to make a better science fair project. Another change is that I am trying to clean my locker every Friday because my friend Sophie said it was becoming a public health situation.

follow_ups.question: What coding project are you working on now?
follow_ups.response: A little wildlife sighting tracker where you can enter an animal, location, and date. It is basic, but I want it to sort entries and maybe graph them.

follow_ups.question: Did your sleep change with activities?
follow_ups.response: Yes, if I have late practice and homework I might not get to bed until 10:00, which makes mornings rough.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I do not have children. I am still a kid myself. If I answer for my brother a little, Tyler goes to elementary school, comes home, has a snack, does homework if my parents make him, and then plays games or draws. He does not have as many activities as me, but he has tried soccer and art club.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever help take care of Tyler?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes I help him with homework or keep an eye on him while my parents are making dinner, but I am not like a babysitter for long periods.

follow_ups.question: Does your schedule affect his?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, because he gets dragged to my games or waits in the car during pickups.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have not had big personal experiences with law enforcement. Mostly I see police at school safety events, parades, traffic stuff, or the county fair. We had an officer come talk at school about internet safety and not sharing personal information online. My parents tell me to be respectful if I ever have to talk to police, but I have never been stopped or anything like that. In a small town you kind of know which families know which officers, so it feels familiar but also official.

follow_ups.question: Have police ever come to your school for an emergency?
follow_ups.response: Not for anything serious that I was part of. We have drills, and sometimes officers are around for safety talks.

follow_ups.question: How do your friends talk about police?
follow_ups.response: Mostly not a lot, unless something is in the news or someone sees a police car near school.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: The school internet safety talk stands out because they talked about screenshots and how online stuff does not disappear. Also police help with traffic at busy school events.

follow_ups.question: Did the internet safety talk change your behavior?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I got more careful about privacy settings and not posting where I am in real time.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever asked an officer a question?
follow_ups.response: At the fair once I asked about the K-9 demonstration, but that was it.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested, and I do not know of anyone close in my family being arrested. I have heard about people in town getting in trouble, but not someone close to me.

follow_ups.question: Has that affected your family directly?
follow_ups.response: No, not directly.

follow_ups.question: Do your parents talk about those situations with you?
follow_ups.response: Only in a general way, like making good choices and not getting in cars with people doing unsafe things.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I cannot vote yet because I am thirteen. My parents vote most of the time, especially for president and local things like school budgets. I hear about elections at home, but I am not the person making those decisions. At school we have student council elections, and I take those seriously because they actually affect us, like dances, fundraisers, and spirit days. I think when I am old enough I will vote because it seems like something you should do if you care about your town.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever helped with a campaign or election?
follow_ups.response: Only student council. I made a little speech and posters, and I tried not to make promises I could not keep.

follow_ups.question: Do you follow national elections?
follow_ups.response: A little through my parents and school, but I do not watch political news every day.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I am still figuring them out, so I would not say I have a full political identity. I care about the environment, animals, schools, and people being treated fairly. Because I live in a rural place, I also understand that people care a lot about jobs, farming, fuel costs, and being able to handle things themselves. In my family, people are practical more than super political, at least around me. My mom talks about health care, schools, and animals, and my dad talks about taxes, roads, and whether leaders actually know what small towns are like. I think I lean toward wanting government to help with things people cannot fix alone, like pollution or school funding, but I also like local control and people knowing their community. On social issues, I think people should be respected and not bullied. I probably sound like a middle school student because I am one, but I pay attention when an issue connects to real people I know.

follow_ups.question: What issue feels most personal to you?
follow_ups.response: Environmental stuff, especially protecting habitats and clean water. I want to work with wildlife or veterinary medicine someday, so that feels connected to my future.

follow_ups.question: Do your friends talk politics?
follow_ups.response: Not in a serious adult way. We talk more about school rules, book bans if they come up, climate change, and things people post online.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I think I have become more aware that issues are complicated. When I was younger I thought if something sounded nice, everyone should just do it. Now I hear adults talk about how programs cost money or how rules affect different people differently. I still care about climate and fairness, but I am learning to ask what the actual plan is. Science class has also made me care more about evidence and not just opinions. I would say my views are becoming more practical, not less caring.

follow_ups.question: What helped you become more practical?
follow_ups.response: Student council, honestly. Planning a food drive sounds simple until you need boxes, announcements, teacher permission, dates, and someone to count everything.

follow_ups.question: Has anyone changed your mind about an issue?
follow_ups.response: My dad has made me think more about how rural people can feel ignored when rules are made far away.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: They have affected me somewhat. Sherburne is mostly White, and I am White, so I do not experience racism myself. But I have seen news stories and school discussions that made me realize people can have very different experiences with police or school discipline depending on race. It is not something I can pretend I fully understand from my own life. In class, when we talk about history or current events, I try to listen instead of acting like I know everything. It has made me more careful about jokes or comments people make because sometimes people say things like they are harmless, but they are not.

follow_ups.question: Where have you learned the most about it?
follow_ups.response: School discussions, news clips my parents watch, and some videos online, though I know online stuff can be dramatic or incomplete.

follow_ups.question: Have you talked about it with friends?
follow_ups.response: A little, mostly when something happens in the news or if someone says something insensitive at school.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the main thing is that people want to be treated fairly and listened to when they say something is wrong. I do not think supporting fairness means hating every police officer, because that seems too simple. But I also do not think you can ignore patterns if a lot of people are saying they have been treated badly. I think schools should teach history honestly, including things that are uncomfortable. Since I am from a place that is not very diverse, I probably need to read and listen more than assume.

follow_ups.question: What does listening look like for you?
follow_ups.response: Not interrupting with, like, 'but that never happens here.' Also checking different sources before repeating something.

follow_ups.question: Do you connect it to school life?
follow_ups.response: Yes, because fairness at school matters too, like who gets believed, who gets in trouble, and who feels welcome.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think race is one of those things where some people want to say it is over because laws changed, but then other people have stories showing it is not over. In my own life, I do not have a lot of close experience with racial diversity, which is something I notice. I have been thinking that being from a mostly White rural town can make it easy to miss things other people deal with every day. I also think online arguments make people defensive fast, so it is hard to have normal conversations. I am trying to be the kind of person who asks questions without making someone else do all the work of teaching me.

follow_ups.question: Has your school covered race in history or English class?
follow_ups.response: Yes, in units about slavery, civil rights, and some current events. It depends on the teacher how deep the conversation gets.

follow_ups.question: What feels hard about those conversations?
follow_ups.response: People get nervous about saying the wrong thing, or they joke because they are uncomfortable.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have talked with family and a few friends, but I have not joined protests. Mostly I listen, ask questions in class, and try to speak up if someone at school says something racist or mean.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever spoken up directly?
follow_ups.response: Once someone made a stereotype joke, and I said it was not funny. It was awkward, but they stopped.

follow_ups.question: Do you post about it online?
follow_ups.response: Not really. I am careful online, and I do not want to post something just to look good.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My parents talk about it carefully. My mom is more likely to say people should listen to experiences different from ours. My dad tends to focus on fairness and facts and not judging a whole group, including police, by one story. My friends are mixed, mostly because some pay attention and some do not. Teachers at school usually try to keep conversations respectful. In Sherburne, I think a lot of people are aware of the topic but not always comfortable talking about it deeply.

follow_ups.question: Do you and your parents disagree?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes about tone or what a news story means, but not in a yelling way.

follow_ups.question: Who has influenced you most on this topic?
follow_ups.response: Probably teachers who connect history to now, because that helps me see patterns instead of just one argument.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: I am pretty healthy overall. I play soccer, hike, and stay active, so my endurance is good. I get normal colds and seasonal allergies sometimes, especially in spring when everything is blooming. I have had sore ankles and knees from soccer, but nothing major right now. I try to eat decently, though I definitely like cookies and pizza. Sleep is the thing I mess up most when I have homework and activities.

follow_ups.question: Do you take any regular medicine?
follow_ups.response: No daily prescriptions. Sometimes allergy medicine if my parents say I need it.

follow_ups.question: How often do you exercise in a normal week?
follow_ups.response: During soccer season, probably four or five days a week if you count practices, games, and conditioning.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: It is easy because I like being active and I have sports built into my week. It is hard because my schedule gets crowded, and then I want quick snacks instead of real food. Winter is harder because it gets dark early and I am inside more. My parents help by keeping normal food in the house and reminding me to sleep. My friends also make exercise more fun because soccer does not feel like a workout the whole time.

follow_ups.question: What snacks do you usually choose?
follow_ups.response: Granola bars, apples, popcorn, or whatever chips are around. Sometimes I forget the wrappers in my locker, which is bad.

follow_ups.question: What healthy habit are you proud of?
follow_ups.response: I drink water at practice and usually pack my gear ahead, so I am not skipping warmups or forgetting stuff.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: I have not had any major diagnosis or broken bone. Last year I rolled my ankle during soccer and had to rest it for a couple weeks, which felt dramatic because I hate sitting out. I went to the doctor, iced it, wore a brace, and did some exercises before going fully back. I also had a bad cold that made me miss a rehearsal, but that was normal kid stuff. The ankle thing taught me that pretending pain is not there just makes coaches and parents more annoyed later.

follow_ups.question: Did the ankle injury change how you play?
follow_ups.response: For a little while I was cautious cutting left, but now I mostly just make sure I warm up right.

follow_ups.question: Were you worried about losing your spot?
follow_ups.response: Yes, even though my coach said not to worry. I felt like if I missed practices, I would fall behind.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: Health has not gotten in the way in a huge way for me. The ankle injury got in the way of soccer for a short time, and being tired can make homework harder, but I do not have a condition that stops me from school or activities.

follow_ups.question: What do you do when you are too tired?
follow_ups.response: I try to do the most urgent homework first and move smaller things to the next day if I can.

follow_ups.question: Do adults notice when you are overdoing it?
follow_ups.response: My mom does. She can tell when I am getting snappy because I need sleep.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Nothing huge in my immediate family right now. My grandparents have normal older-person health things, like blood pressure and sore joints, so sometimes plans change if they are not feeling up to something.
